title: Law and story
hook: the Talmud mixes law (halakha) and story (aggadah) on the same page

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel's seven rules, and your line: rules for reading. Light and heavy, the same word, learning from context. Tools for law. But the Talmud doesn't only do law. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

Rabbi Yose is on the road, and it's time to pray. He steps into a ruin, one of the broken buildings of Jerusalem, for a quiet corner. When he comes out, someone is waiting at the doorway. It's Elijah the prophet, who has stood there patiently until the prayer was done. Elijah has two questions. Why did you go in there? And then: my son, what did you hear? One answer leads to a rule about prayer. The other is something no legal argument could hold. This story isn't in a book of tales. It sits in the middle of a discussion about the hours of the night. Today's word is the kind of thing it is.
screen: `A RABBI IN A RUIN.` → `ELIJAH AT THE DOORWAY.` → `WHAT DID YOU HEAR?`

segments.voice: Aggadah. The Talmud's stories, sayings, parables and reflections: everything that isn't law. The law has its own name: halakha. And here's the surprise for a first-time reader. They aren't in separate books. They share the page. Start with where we are. Early in tractate Berakhot, the sages are working out when the evening Shema may be said, and that leads to a question about how the night is divided into watches. A legal question, about time. Then a sage teaches that at each watch of the night, God roars like a lion over the destroyed Temple. And right there, Rabbi Yose tells his story. Elijah's first words to him are practical. Why go into a ruin? You could have prayed on the road. And if passersby might interrupt, a short prayer is enough. Rabbi Yose draws the rules out plainly: don't go into a ruin; you may pray on the road; on the road, keep it short. Then Elijah asks what he heard. A heavenly voice, Rabbi Yose says, cooing like a dove, mourning: woe to the children, because of whose sins I destroyed my house and sent them into exile. Elijah tells him this isn't the only time the voice is heard. Notice what just happened. Rules about prayer and a story of grief, in one conversation, at one doorway. The legal page and the story page are one page. Why keep them together? One reading: law tells you what to do at a given hour of the night, and story tells you why the night matters at all. Without the law, the story floats. Without the story, the law can go cold. The Talmud keeps them in the same breath. Story and law together.
screen: `AGGADAH: WHAT ISN'T LAW.` · `A LEGAL QUESTION ABOUT THE NIGHT.` · `RULES AT THE DOORWAY.` · `A VOICE LIKE A DOVE.` · then, large: `STORY AND LAW TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to read one Talmud story. You just heard one, so let it settle. Sit, and breathe. See the broken walls. See the man praying alone, and the figure waiting at the doorway, not interrupting. Hear, if you can, a sound like a dove. Now notice what the doorway held: a rule you can keep, pray where it's safe and keep it short on the road, and a grief no rule can hold. Ask yourself whether any habit or rule in your own life carries a story like that underneath. The bell holds the time.
Aggadah. The Talmud's stories, sayings and reflections, the part that isn't law, sharing the page with halakha. Today's word.
Your line: story and law together. Today, pick one rule you keep, at home or at work, and find the story behind it. Tell it to someone, or just remember it. Day one thousand ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Students learn the Talmud's aggadah in the same study session as its legal discussions, since they appear together on the page; some collections, like the Ein Yaakov, gather the stories on their own.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Yose. you've just come out of a ruin where you prayed, and Elijah is waiting at the door. what does Elijah say first?
options: praise you for finding a holy place to pray.
ask why you went in: you could have prayed on the road, briefly.
fork.reveal: Elijah starts with practical advice: don't enter a ruin; you may pray on the road; a short prayer is enough there. only then does he ask what you heard. law and story at one doorway.

original.note: Hebrew: the Talmud's stories and sayings; in Ashkenazi pronunciation, ah-GAH-dah.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Talmud's stories are side decorations.
what it means: aggadah shares the page with halakha, and each needs the other.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 3a, where the night watches lead into God roaring like a lion and Rabbi Yose's encounter with Elijah: rulings on prayer in ruins and on the road, then the dove-voice.

notes: Berakhot 3a is paraphrased throughout: the night watches, 'at each watch the Holy One roars like a lion', Rabbi Yose in the ruin, the bat kol cooing like a dove, and Elijah's advice. Please confirm the order and that 'this isn't the only time the voice is heard' fairly condenses Elijah's reply.
The common gloss of halakha as 'the way to walk' is deliberately left out, under the claims rule.
The Ein Yaakov is named in howItsDone as a collection of the Talmud's aggadah; please confirm.
This day continues the Berakhot thread from days 1092–1093 on purpose.

Editor: fixed the order of Berakhot 3a. Elijah first asks why Rabbi Yose entered the ruin and gives the practical advice (pray on the road, a short prayer), from which Rabbi Yose learns three things; only then does Elijah ask what voice he heard. The script had the voice first and the advice after ('the story turns back into law'). Hook, teach, screen, practice, myth, fork and trapdoor were adjusted to match.
